passages.t: Esther before the king, and a banquet
passages.happening:
‘On the third day, Esther put on her royal attire and stood in the inner court of the palace across from the king’s quarters’ (verse 1). The king is on his throne, facing the entrance.

‘As soon as the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she found favor in his sight. The king extended the gold scepter in his hand toward Esther, and she approached and touched the tip of the scepter’ (verse 2). “What is it, Queen Esther?” the king inquired. “What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom, it will be given to you” (verse 3).

But Esther does not make her request yet. “If it pleases the king,” Esther replied, “may the king and Haman come today to the banquet I have prepared for the king” (verse 4). They come, and as they drink their wine, the king asks again. Again she waits. She asks them to come to a second banquet tomorrow, ‘Then I will answer the king’s question’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Esther ended chapter 4 by resolving to go to the king though it might cost her life. Here the danger passes in two verses: she finds favor, and the scepter is held out. But the rescue is not done, and the story slows down on purpose.

The king sits in a royal hall facing the entrance, as in what is known of Persian audience halls, large columned rooms where the king was seen from a distance and approached with ceremony. The offer of up to half the kingdom was a formula of royal generosity, not a literal promise.

To invite the king to a meal she had prepared was to honor him and to draw him into a setting where a request could be made gracefully. The double invitation keeps the king curious and shows that her request is serious. It also puts Haman, the enemy, at the queen's table, where he can be exposed. Esther acts with patience and discretion, not haste.
passages.later: The same royal formula is spoken in the Gospels, when Herod Antipas swears to a dancer, “Whatever you ask of me, I will give you, up to half my kingdom!” (Mark 6:23).
passages.asks: Esther had the king's attention and still waited for the right moment. Ask whether you are quick to speak when patience would serve better. And ask how you might prepare the ground, as she did, before you ask for something that matters.

passages.t: Haman at home, and a gallows
passages.happening:
‘That day Haman went out full of joy and glad of heart’ (verse 9). But at the king's gate he sees Mordecai, who will not rise or tremble before him, and he is filled with rage. He holds himself back and goes home.

He calls his friends and his wife Zeresh and tells them of his wealth, his many sons, and every honor the king has given him. “What is more,” Haman added, “Queen Esther invited no one but me to join the king at the banquet she prepared, and I am invited back tomorrow along with the king” (verse 12). “Yet none of this satisfies me as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate” (verse 13).

His wife and friends advise him: build a gallows fifty cubits high, and ask the king in the morning to have Mordecai hanged on it. ‘The advice pleased Haman, and he had the gallows constructed’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Haman's speech shows how honor worked in an ancient court. Wealth, many sons and promotion over other officials were the visible measures of a man's standing, and a public slight from someone below him could feel unbearable.

He has everything, and one man's refusal to bow empties all of it. Pride always needs more, and hatred makes a man reckless.

The gallows is fifty cubits high. A cubit was the length of a forearm, roughly eighteen inches, so the structure would be about seventy-five feet tall, a height meant to be seen across the city. The Hebrew word is simply tree or wood, and many scholars think it means a tall pole for executing or displaying a body rather than a gallows with a rope. The book does not dwell on it, and these notes do not either.

The irony runs through the scene. Haman boasts that he alone is invited with the king, not knowing that the invitation is a trap, and he ends the day pleased with a gallows that will be used for him.
passages.later: A psalm says what the book will show: ‘He has dug a hole and hollowed it out; he has fallen into a pit of his own making’ (Psalm 7:15).
passages.asks: Haman had wealth, family and honor, and none of it satisfied him while one man would not bow. Ask what grudge is spoiling good things in your own life. And ask what you would have to let go of to be content.
